title: Reasons for Action: Agent-Neutral vs. Agent-Relative

summaries.example: Imagine you can call either your best friend or a stranger. If your reason is that the call would make anyone happy, the reason is agent-neutral: it does not depend on who you are. If your reason is that the call would help your own friend, the reason is agent-relative: your relationship matters. Philosophers also ask whether a reason can change in different situations. A fact that helps in one situation might not help in another if an important difference defeats it.
summaries.summary: The entry explains two ways reasons for action can be connected to people. An agent-neutral reason is based on a rule that does not make a special reference to the person who has the reason. An agent-relative reason does make such a reference—for example, to that person’s own welfare or family. The entry compares three ways to draw this line. A principle-based approach looks at the form of the rule behind a reason. A reason-statement approach looks at how the reason itself must be described. A perspective-based approach asks whether the reason can be understood from a more detached point of view. Each approach has difficulties. The entry supports a revised principle-based view using “default principles.” These rules say that a consideration normally gives a reason unless some feature of the situation defeats it. This lets philosophers recognize that reasons can depend on context while still asking whether the reason is tied specially to the agent. The distinction matters because it helps organize debates about self-interest, helping others, moral rules, and different kinds of moral theory.
key_ideas: Some reasons apply without giving special importance to the person who has them; others depend on that person’s relationships, interests, or aims.
Philosophers have explained the difference using principles, complete statements of reasons, or points of view.
The entry favors a carefully revised principle-based account that can allow a reason to change with its situation.
Agent-neutral and agent-relative are not the same as other pairs, such as internal and external reasons or universal and non-universal reasons.
summaries.why_it_matters: When people argue about what someone ought to do, they may disagree about whether the reason belongs especially to that person or could guide anyone in a relevantly similar situation. Keeping these ideas apart helps us understand debates about fairness, friendship, self-interest, consequences, and moral rules. It also reminds us not to confuse agent-relativity with simply having a personal opinion or with a reason that someone happens to understand better.

important_terms.definition: A consideration that counts in favor of doing something.
A reason whose basic rule does not depend in a special way on the person who has it.
A reason whose basic rule refers in a special way to the person who has it, such as that person’s friend or welfare.
A general guide about when something counts as a reason.
The idea that a reason can work differently in different situations.

questions_to_think_about: If helping someone would make them happy, does it matter whether they are your friend?
Can the same fact be a reason in one situation but not in another?
Should a rule about your own welfare apply to every person in the same way?
Why might it be confusing to call every personal reason “private”?

summaries.example: Suppose two policies both aim to increase happiness. One says that an agent has reason to choose the option that increases overall happiness. Its reason is agent-neutral because the relevant value does not refer non-trivially to that agent. Another says that an agent has reason to choose what increases that agent’s own welfare. Its reason is agent-relative. The distinction is not identical to the difference between internal and external reasons: a person’s culture or biological needs might provide an agent-relative reason even if the person does not desire to follow them. Nor is it identical to whether a reason is shared, universal, or communicable.
summaries.summary: The entry investigates the distinction between agent-relative and agent-neutral reasons for action. On the influential principle-based conception, a reason is agent-relative when the principle associated with it refers non-trivially to the agent who has the reason—for instance, to that agent’s welfare, projects, or special relations. It is agent-neutral when the principle does not contain that kind of reference. The entry also examines a reason-statement-based proposal, which classifies a reason by whether its full description requires an indexical reference such as “his” or “her.” This proposal may depend too heavily on controversial views about what reasons are. A perspective-based proposal classifies reasons by whether they can be recognized from an objective standpoint, but this risks making the classification depend on disputed theories of objectivity and may fail to classify paradigmatic egoistic reasons decisively. The preferred revision keeps the principle-based structure but replaces strict universality with default principles. Such principles allow defeaters and therefore fit holistic or particularist views, according to which a consideration may support an action in one context but lose its force in another. The account must exclude merely trivial references to the agent, such as the fact that the agent must be able to perform the action. The distinction is valuable because it clarifies debates about consequentialism and deontology, egoism, special obligations, expressivism, and the relation between value and reasons.
key_ideas: The three historical approaches are principle-based, reason-statement-based, and perspective-based; they do not simply express the same test in different words.
The revised principle-based approach removes a strong universality assumption and uses default principles, making room for moral particularism.
A trivial reference to an agent’s ability to perform an action should not make every reason agent-relative; the relevant reference must be non-trivial.
Agent-relativity differs from internal/external reasons, universality, generality, deliberator-relative authority, appraiser-relativity, and essentially shared reasons.
The distinction helps analyze whether egoistic, deontological, consequentialist, or special-relationship reasons have different structures.
The classification of a reason can be surprising: for example, expected-utility theories may involve agent-relative reasons because the relevant expectations are the agent’s.
summaries.why_it_matters: The distinction is a framework for comparing normative theories, not merely a label for selfish and unselfish behavior. It can show how two theories with similar aims differ in logical structure, and it can reveal why arguments about consequences, restrictions, integrity, or special relationships take different forms. The entry’s careful revision also illustrates a broader philosophical lesson: a useful distinction should separate cases before the major dispute is settled, rather than define the cases by appeal to a controversial conclusion.

important_terms.definition: A consideration that counts in favor of an action, or a normative basis for saying someone has something to do.
A reason whose associated principle contains no non-trivial reference to the agent for whom it is a reason.
A reason whose associated principle contains a non-trivial reference to that agent, such as the agent’s welfare or special relationships.
A rule or general form that explains when a consideration supports an action.
A hedged rule saying a consideration is normally a reason unless some feature of the situation defeats it.
The view that a consideration can be a reason in one context but not in another, because the surrounding facts alter its normative force.
A feature that prevents a consideration from functioning as a reason in a particular case.
A condition that must be present for another consideration to function as a reason.

questions_to_think_about: Does a reason to protect your own welfare differ in structure from a reason to increase welfare generally?
Can a principle remain useful if it allows that unknown features of a situation may defeat a reason?
Why should agent-relativity not be defined merely by the fact that an action is possible for one agent?
Could a moral restriction be understood as a teleological, or outcome-related, reason that is nevertheless agent-relative?
What would be lost if agent-relative reasons were confused with reasons based on personal desire?

summaries.example: Maya is deciding whether to spend an afternoon helping at a community garden or helping her younger brother study. A reason such as “the garden will improve the neighborhood” might be agent-neutral if the rule gives the same kind of reason to anyone who can help. A reason such as “my brother needs my help” may be agent-relative because it depends on Maya’s special relationship. But context can matter too: if the garden project is secretly harming people, the fact that it helps the neighborhood may no longer be a reason. A revised rule can say that a fact is normally a reason unless something in the situation defeats it.
summaries.summary: This entry studies a philosophical difference between agent-relative and agent-neutral reasons. A reason is agent-relative when the principle supporting it makes a non-trivial reference to the person who has it—for example, that an action benefits that person or helps someone specially connected to them. A reason is agent-neutral when the supporting principle does not depend in that way on the identity or relationships of the agent. The entry explains three major approaches. The principle-based approach looks at the general rule behind a reason. The reason-statement-based approach looks at whether the reason itself must be described using a reference back to the agent. The perspective-based approach looks at whether the reason can be understood from a suitably objective viewpoint. Each approach has problems. The perspective approach may make familiar examples, such as self-interest, depend on controversial claims about objectivity. The reason-statement approach may rely on controversial ideas about whether reasons are facts, propositions, or facts presented in a particular way. The entry recommends a modified principle-based approach. It uses default principles, which say that a consideration is normally a reason unless some feature of the situation explains why it is not. This allows the account to respect particularism, the view that reasons can change with context. The distinction matters because it gives philosophers a way to analyze moral theories and arguments without confusing agent-relativity with other ideas such as desire, universality, or personal opinion.
key_ideas: The distinction asks whether the rule behind a reason refers specially to the person who has that reason.
A principle-based account examines the rule connected with the reason; a reason-statement account examines how the reason must be fully described.
A perspective-based account asks whether a reason can be recognized from a more objective standpoint, but this may depend on controversial ideas about objectivity.
The revised principle-based account uses default principles, so it can accept that reasons sometimes change when circumstances change.
Agent-relative does not simply mean personal, desired, private, or subjective; several other philosophical distinctions can cross-cut it.
The distinction helps philosophers compare self-interest, concern for everyone, moral restrictions, and special duties.
summaries.why_it_matters: The distinction helps explain why two people might have different reasons without simply saying that one of them is biased. It also helps compare theories about maximizing good results, protecting personal integrity, following restrictions, or giving special attention to family and friends. Understanding the distinction prevents philosophical arguments from talking past one another, especially when words like “objective,” “relative,” or “shared” are being used in different ways.

important_terms.definition: A fact or consideration that supports choosing one action rather than another.
A reason that does not depend on a special fact about the particular person who has it.
A reason that depends on a special fact about the person who has it, such as that person’s needs or relationships.
A general rule used to explain why a fact counts in favor of an action.
A rule that says something is usually a reason, while allowing an important situation-specific exception.
The view that a reason’s force can depend on the surrounding circumstances.
A reason that normally supports an action but is blocked by another fact in a particular case.
A condition that helps another fact count as a reason.

questions_to_think_about: Is “helping my sibling” agent-relative because of the relationship, or could it also be described in a neutral way?
Why might a philosopher prefer a rule with exceptions to a rule that lists every possible exception?
Can a reason be agent-relative even when the person does not want to follow it?
How is a reason about the person judging an action different from a reason about the person performing it?
Why is it risky to decide that all moral disagreements are just disagreements between different perspectives?
